I really got so addicted to another game called Tunnet that I literally had to peel myself away from the thing. =P Anyway, having that good experience with network builders, I came here looking for another hit of the good stuff. Well OK, this game gives you a vaguely realistic set of networking equipment, though the problem of maintaining adequate DNS service was far far far worse than IRL. Still, I wanted to give the game the benefit of the doubt, it's in early access after all! I tried the game in its campaign mode first, I did ok, but really wasn't satisfied. I then put the game in grins and giggles mode so I could see more of what it had to offer with much less stress. I am writing this having gotten to nearly the 40th floor in that mode and I'm really coming to realize how deeply flawed this game is, even if the balance issues were addressed I think this runs too deep to fix. The game has the player as a juggler, who can't hire more staff, but has an endlessly increasing number of plates to keep spinning on sticks or it's game over. Even if half there weren't so many problems with the UI and animations, the game also has an element of hard randomness. As the DNS barely works, you are obliged to upgrade it as quickly as humanly possible but the upgrade is locked behind a random number generator that governs which "proposals" are available to work on. So I guess you can treat it as a sport, to see how high in the tower you can climb, or you could go search for (or write) a game that lets you build a network you can be proud of.

About two hours in, and I’m still not sure what to make of this game. I have zero experience setting up a network and honestly, even after a couple of hours, I still don’t. I’m almost through the tutorial section, but I still have no idea what I’m actually doing half the time. To be fair, I know it’s Early Access, and for £16 it’s not terrible value though I do think £10 or slightly less would feel more appropriate right now. The game runs smoothly, but the UI really needs work. The brown tablet interface and cluttered icons are hard on the eyes, and the red text is nearly impossible to read. Tutorial-wise, it’s okay in structure, but it doesn’t explain why you’re doing things. Why am I scanning the DNS again? What exactly does a switch do? For a complete beginner who loves logic-based management games, I’m struggling to make sense of it all. That’s not necessarily the game’s fault it’s just not beginner-friendly yet. I’m really on the fence. On one hand, when I finally figure something out, I feel like a genius. On the other, I feel completely lost and dumb. Deep down, I want to get better at this because I can see the potential for it to be a great, chill, brain-stimulating game. I’m even debating whether to refund it or stick with it might just sleep on that decision. If I could give one piece of feedback to the devs: focus on improving the tutorial for new players and redesign the tablet interface with clearer, more readable icons and colours. Also, a simple cable management tool (like a hook or organizer) would be a great quality-of-life addition. I might give this another try later. For now, I’m giving it a thumbs down because it’s really tough for a beginner. If I do refund it, I’ll probably come back to it in a few years once it’s more polished. But if I stick with it and reach around 20 hours of playtime, I’ll come back and update this review to share how I got on.

This game is terrifying. I don't know what damage I was born with that makes networking like catnip to me, but this scratches some itch I barely knew I had. I went from wondering why Steam was even recommending it to me to logging 10 hours within 2 days. I will say, I think some people need to embrace the rougelike nature a little more. It's not a game about making 1 very good network, it's a game about throwing yourself at different problems over and over and doing the best you can do at the time. At my playtime I still can't keep a tower going for more than about 2 weeks on standard difficulty. You [i]will[/i] lose, but that's what the new game button is for. And, seriously, don't be afraid to bump it down to easy or play on the Zen mode for no time pressure. I don't know who the hell is playing this on Hard. I assume they work at Cisco. Give it a try. For the price, there's a hell of a lot to like here. Feedback for the devs? Love the variety in floors higher up. I'd like to see more of that early on. It seems like we're limited to basic apartments and ~3 types of offices for a really long time, until the point that for players to see anything else they've probably already sunk 20 hours into the game. Having to make it 40 days into a save to unlock new floor types is an insane hurdle.

In summary: If you just want to use it as a fun tool, such as testing how many devices a switch can connect, or if you're a beginner: don't buy it, especially if you don't know the difference between a switch and a router. It's not worth 76 yuan. It does have advantages: unique theme, pixel art style, realistic physics simulation, individual cable modeling, various accessories and users, and detailed item textures. You can even manually turn devices on and off. However, the disadvantages are: very limited physics settings, leading to significant lag in the later stages; cable physics can also malfunction randomly; worst of all, after prolonged play, the physics may completely break down, requiring a game restart. There are several modes, but I don't recommend any except the intern mode. The original equipment has a very high failure rate. Power outages occur every two days. If you manually change the settings, you'll lose your achievements. The initial stages are the most frustrating. There are cheap devices, but they look like they were picked up from a junkyard, with performance equivalent to a Pentium 2. If you dare use them, expect random fire and overload. Other, even the more expensive ones, have performance disproportionate to their price, forcing you to spend most of your money on upgrading equipment, which is where the real problem lies. The worst part is yet to come. The cost of connecting each floor is outrageously high; yes, even connecting each floor costs extra. Spending hundreds or thousands of dollars per day per floor means you can't even recoup your investment, and what do you get in return? A 40kbps fiber optic connection constantly overloaded. The service provider is deliberately designed to annoy you; the bandwidth is always stuck at 81 or 82kbps. Upgrading is impossible, and the connection is neither lag-prone nor completely unusable. You either upgrade to a 140kbps fiber optic cable costing 1000kbps per day, or you get yelled at every day. Users are also demanding, wanting this and that, and turning on you the moment there's a lag. After the sixth floor, these bastards have no peace. The fees are based on the lowest possible satisfaction level; they deduct money whenever they're unhappy. The problem is, you have to give them more! Users on each floor can barely afford the daily internet cable fee, let alone the service you're building yourself. You then have two choices: either you endure it and collect a pittance, since nobody benefits anyway, but then all the equipment suddenly breaks down simultaneously, you spend a fortune on repairs, and the SLA is running too fast to be repaired in time; or you accumulate a mountain of debt and are gloriously fired. Either you're determined to make major changes, but end up notifying people of too many network outages, and when the connection drops, the SLA runs too fast to keep up; or you upgrade your equipment, incur a mountain of debt, and get fired. The game's kill threshold is definitely there. In short, the balance is a complete mess, and don't expect official optimization. If this hasn't already deterred you: Tutorials are almost nonexistent; I know about VLANs and patch notes. Some aren't even translated, and those that are are machine-translated—judge the quality yourself, since it's free. The network cable is extremely short, and I don't understand why extenders have bandwidth limitations. The physics simulation is incredibly abstract; items slide randomly and then fall apart, and the cable jerks at low frame rates. In short, don't treat it as a serious game. The game is very niche; there are almost no tutorials available, either domestically or internationally. The game is still in development. I joined the Discord channel, but the feedback isn't very active. The official version hasn't been updated in a long time. If you want to experience more, select "beta" in the properties. Someone posted a cheat mod on Discord, but it's broken in the latest version. It seems the developers don't want you to modify the game; Cheat Engine can't find the money. I've always been lenient with small development teams, until my save file went bankrupt, and I could only watch helplessly. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

题材很喜欢，看到就马上入手了。 实际体验下来有点一言难尽。 首先中文翻译不完全是小事，但是翻译不上心，机翻味太重，格式处理也很有问题，名词不统一，看着很累，后面干脆切到英文玩了。 然后说说游戏本体： 作为单纯的游戏来说太硬核，引导不够，wiki 的排版和编排太差了，查的的时候很费劲。确实有一个引导关卡教学怎么起步，但是真上手开荒了还是云里雾里。客户的满意度也看不出来为什么忽然会掉一点，排查很困难。而且游戏太注重资源规划了，我花了大量的时间测量和购买网线和电源线…这没什么问题，但是每个玩家体验的侧重点不太一样，我对这款游戏的预期不是在这些事情上花大量时间。 作为网工模拟器来说，跟现实的差距又是不可忽视的。首先游戏前期没有网段的概念，所以我在选择用路由器还是交换机上就觉得实际上完全没有必要使用路由器。但是实际上这个交换机是个换壳集线器，收到的数据包都会广播出去…至于造成的影响，我能感受到应该是存在的，但是很难直接表现出来。而如果使用路由器，因为没有网段，所以如果配置每家每户的路由的话工作量就太大了，缺少一个[b]真正的[/b]交换机作为中间层。 然后想吐槽一下，我有些过早优化和过度抽象的恶癖，所以开局就想搭建一个好扩展的物理框架和网络结构，但是一看机柜有三种尺寸？？？这真的是必要的游戏设计吗？ 归根结底还是引导做得不直观，期待游戏能慢慢变好。

This game convinced me to go back and finish getting my CCNA. A lot of fun. It still needs some polish and balancing passes, but if you like games in the vein of Turing Complete, this is a fun one for networking and server administration and operations. It's like a gamier version of Packet Tracer, almost. The multiplayer is also surprisingly fun. You'd think there's a lot of stepping on toes but with difficulty settings you can just put each person in charge of different tasks. My only real gripes are: 1. Switches seem to function like hubs. They don't maintain a mac (or I guess hardware, in game terminology) address table and so they forward all traffic out of every port, which means they quickly overwhelm bandwidth. It feels like other than needing to deal with setting up routing tables, this means that routers are pretty much strictly better than switches until you get vlan-enabled switches. 2. The RFP system feels a bit odd at the moment. Locking stuff like sftp, which is necessary if you made a misstep and allowed a worm to hit your routers, behind random chance feels punishing. It almost feels like this should be split into an RFP system which provides run modifiers (like the Tenabolt-related proposals) and a tech tree that grants access to core stuff (maybe something like hub -> switch upgrades, other device upgrades, sftp, and other semi-essential stuff). Still though, these are relatively minor issues, and I've already seen enough content added in updates that these are far from deal breakers.
